profile.story: Walt Kowalski is 63 and has run a precision machining job shop in Grand Rapids since 1994 — fourteen CNC machines, 26 people, AS9100 certified, $4.02M of revenue at a 34% gross margin. He quotes every job himself off a shop rate sheet dated 2021, the average quote takes eleven days to go out, and the shop wins 26% of what it quotes. There is a Haas VF-4 that has been idle for fourteen months because, in Walt's telling, there is nobody to run it. Asked about AI and automation he was flat: 'We don't do AI. There is no AI in a machine shop and there isn't going to be.'

edge_cases: DESIGNED TO FAIL THE GATE: four N/As in the Leverage pillar (L6, L7, L9, L10) with 'we don't do it' reasons, which Rubrics v2 §5 does not permit
the harness should mark Leverage insufficient data, exclude it from the composite, renormalise Profit and Systems to 0.40/0.35 of 0.75, and BLOCK release

everything else in the file is complete and clean — 14 Demonstrated/Documented indicators, notes on every score, constraint and cost present, three ordered opportunities — so the Leverage N/As are the only blocker
one included opportunity is an automation build in a pillar that has been excluded — the reviewer should notice the contradiction

documents.name: AS9100 procedures and 2026 surveillance audit report

P1.note: Four sources named with monthly volume, and the RFQ logbook summary (Doc) gives 408 RFQs and $6.4M quoted for the year — real counts, kept in a paper book and typed up quarterly. Cost known only for the $300 directory listing.
P1.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs the volume logged in one place; it is a handwritten book transcribed once a quarter, and nothing is broken out by source or part family (q25).

P2.note: An RFQ is acknowledged the same day, printed, and put in a physical stack on Walt's desk. The quote itself averages eleven days. No log beyond the paper book; watched the stack in session.
P2.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs the inquiry usually resolved within a day and some capture; the acknowledgement is same-day but the response the customer is actually waiting for takes eleven, and two buyers award at three.

P3.note: q24: Dana calls once about a week after a quote goes out, 'so maybe half get a second contact'. No sequence, no record of which quotes were chased.
P3.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs follow-up that happens across most quotes even person-dependently; half of a $6.4M quote book gets one call and nobody can say which half.

P4.note: 26% close on quoted dollars, computed by Dana from the logbook each quarter and confirmed in the RFQ summary (Doc). Loss reason known anecdotally — price and quote lateness. No stages: q25, 'there is a stack on my desk and I work through it'.
P4.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs stages defined and used and loss reasons captured; there is no process at all, and the close rate is a quarterly backward look rather than a tracked number.

P5.note: Shop rate sheet opened in session, last modified March 2021 (Doc). It is genuinely cost-based — machine-hour rates built off 2021 burden — which is why this is not a 0. One change since: a 2023 material surcharge, reason anecdotal. Expedite premiums applied 'when I remember'. The same P&L shows direct labor up 19% since that sheet was written.
P5.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs some current economics and occasional reviews; the economics are five years stale and there is no job cost (P9) to refresh them from.

P6.note: q29: 'We quote what is on the print.' No bundles, no tiers, no entry offer. Expedite is the only variant and it is applied inconsistently. Fixturing and tooling — 12% of revenue at 38% margin — pulls production work behind it and is never offered proactively.
P6.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs add-ons offered ad hoc by the team; here nothing is offered unless the print asks for it.

P7.note: q27: roughly 80% of customers who order once order again, and blanket POs mostly renew. Both figures are impressions. Inactive customers are not identified — 'I could tell you some names off the top of my head' — and no reactivation has ever been run.
P7.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs a repeat rate measured and an inactive list pulled and worked twice a year; the rate is a memory and the list does not exist.

P8.note: q30: marketing owner 'Nobody', sales owner 'Me', $300/mo, and nothing reviewed together. Dana's quarterly quote summary is the only measurement in the growth engine and it goes to one reader.
P8.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs named owners and numbers reviewed at least sometimes; there is one de-facto owner and one quarterly report nobody discusses.

P9.note: Gross margin 34% confirmed on the 24-month P&L, and margin by line is estimated in q13 from Walt's judgement. JobBOSS collects the hours from paper time cards and the job-costing report has never been run — confirmed by opening it in session.
P9.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs margin by job type known and used; the shop has been capturing the data required for five years and has never once looked at it, which is why the 2021 rate sheet has never been challenged.

P10.note: q20 'Monthly, delayed' — 24 monthly P&Ls on file, produced by an outside bookkeeper four to six weeks out. Walt reads them. q21 carries a revenue and a margin target and 'No target' on profit, cash and owner pay.
P10.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs a close inside 30 days and a routine owner review; the numbers land too late to change a quarter.

S1.note: Dennis genuinely runs the floor and Ron owns quality sign-off. Everything else — q50 lists eleven of eleven categories — returns to Walt, including scheduling exceptions, purchasing, and every price. Watched three interruptions during Block 1, two of them material questions.
S1.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs several areas delegated with money, hiring and exceptions the remaining owner-only set; here purchasing, scheduling and technical decisions are also his.

S2.note: q51 four-week test: released work keeps running about three weeks on Dennis's board; standard bar stock gets reordered; quoting stops on day one and every price and money decision stacks up. Longest actual absence twelve days, and he quoted three jobs from a hospital bed.
S2.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs a named deputy and a few owner-locked items; there is no deputy on price or purchasing, and the shop's forward order book stops the day he does.

S3.note: Dana can quote a repeat part number off the existing sheet. Every new print, every price and every customer conversation is Walt's, and q14 puts ~70% of revenue on buyers who call him personally.
S3.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs the team selling with owner rescue on big deals; nobody else has ever priced a new part or spoken to a buyer about money.

S4.note: Two real managers: Dennis on the floor for nineteen years and Ron on quality — and Ron genuinely owns an outcome, the Delvane OTD number, because the customer's scorecard forces one. q38: 'Mostly clear, with gaps.' Dennis owns no number.
S4.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs managers owning outcomes and metrics; one of two does, and the metric was imposed by a customer rather than chosen by the business.

S5.note: The AS9100 quality system is documented, current and externally audited — the 2026 surveillance report shows no major findings, and the cert-packet process was walked end to end. Everything commercial is undocumented: quoting, purchasing, scheduling and job release exist only in three people's habits. q35: 40% documented, 30% current, 25% used in training.
S5.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs core workflows documented and current; the only current documentation is the part an auditor checks, and the workflow that sets margin has none.

S6.note: A morning production meeting happens daily at the whiteboard — attended, and it is scheduling only. One KPI exists, on-time delivery, owned by Ron and visible on the Delvane scorecard pinned in quality. q39: 'On anything else there is no number to miss.'
S6.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs 3–7 owned KPIs with visible targets; there is one, and it belongs to a customer's scorecard rather than the shop's.

S7.note: Quality is genuinely consistent — AS9100 audited, 94% OTD on the Delvane scorecard, first-article and in-process inspection defined. But q31 says +20% needs 'equipment or capital', q36 lists scheduling delays and rework, and there is a machine that has sat idle for fourteen months.
S7.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs +20% to strain rather than break and QC steps defined across the work; the QC is defined only where the standard requires it, and there is no capacity plan — the response to more demand has been to buy a machine and leave it wrapped.

S8.note: Delvane Aerospace 22% of revenue on the revenue-by-customer report; top five 61% across 38 active customers. v2 anchor 1 is 20–30%.
S8.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs 15–20%. At 22% this sits under the 25% overlay — a watch item — but the top-five figure of 61% is the number that should worry the shop more, and Delvane also carries the certification case.

S9.note: Blanket PO roster (Doc): eleven open blankets covering 58% of revenue, with roughly 80% of customers reordering. q27 is explicit that blankets are forecasts rather than commitments, and q12 records 0% contracted revenue.
S9.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs recurring or contracted revenue covering fixed costs or ≥40% of revenue plus a rolling forecast; the volume is real but uncommitted and no forecast is maintained anywhere.

S10.note: q53: vendor agreements, insurance and employment agreements current, no known legal issue. Against that: the customer 'contracts' are the customers' own terms and conditions, the shop has none of its own, pricing history is 'in my head and in a drawer' (q51), Dennis's schedule is a whiteboard he holds from memory, and there is no continuity plan for a 63-year-old sole owner.
S10.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs some contracts written and known key-person gaps; the gaps are known but nothing is written on the shop's side and no cross-training has begun.

L1.note: JobBOSS ERP is a real system and does real work — order entry, time collection, travelers. QuickBooks Desktop and Paychex behind it. But q41 reads 'none' for CRM, marketing and reporting, quoting is Excel, scheduling is a magnetic whiteboard, and the JobBOSS scheduling module was opened in session and has never been configured.
L1.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 allows one significant gap; quoting, scheduling and reporting are three, and two of them are modules already paid for and never turned on.

L2.note: Paper time cards are keyed into JobBOSS daily (4.6 h/wk, watched at the shop office desk) and JobBOSS totals are typed into QuickBooks monthly. Certs are scanned and indexed by hand into a separate Excel sheet.
L2.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs some genuine integrations alongside the double entry; there are none — every join between systems is a person retyping on a schedule.

L3.note: q43: data generally accurate and backups exist. The OTD number is trusted because a customer audits it. Everything else needs rebuilding by hand: the quote summary quarterly, the OTD scorecard monthly at 3.0 h/wk, and there is no agreed definition of job margin because no job has a cost.
L3.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs agreed KPI definitions and reports needing only light cleanup; one number is trusted, it was defined by a customer, and every other report is built from scratch.

L4.note: 23.5 h/wk inventoried across five tasks (q44), every one flagged for errors. The largest is the 9.7 h/wk quote package — we watched one built from scratch in 2 hours 25 minutes. Nothing has been reduced; the JobBOSS modules that would reduce two of these were bought and never configured.
L4.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs a few fixes actually made; the tools to make them are already licensed and untouched.

L5.note: q45: Paychex runs payroll unattended and the machines have tool-life counters. Both were set up by vendors, neither is owned by anyone here, and that is the complete list.
L5.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs a few automations across the business with mixed reliability; there are two and neither is the shop's.

L6.note: Owner's reason, recorded verbatim: 'We don't do AI. There is no AI in a machine shop and there isn't going to be.' q46 answered 'None'.

L7.note: Owner's reason, recorded verbatim: 'Nothing to govern. We have no AI and no automation, so the discipline question doesn't apply to us.' q47 left empty.

L9.note: Owner's reason, recorded verbatim: 'The team isn't going to use these tools, so readiness isn't a real question here.' q58 answered 'No training, and there is resistance'; q59 says half the machinists do not use the JobBOSS terminal already on the floor.

L8.note: q48: inconsistent backups, no tested recovery, unclear account ownership, one-person dependence. Individual Windows logins on the office machines and a nightly copy to a second server that nobody has ever restored from. The print archive is four filing cabinets and one network folder.
L8.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs partial hygiene with known gaps being managed; the backup is assumed and has never been tested, which is the anchor-1 wording exactly.

L10.note: Owner's reason, recorded verbatim: 'We're not doing a technology project, so there's nothing to have capacity for.' q49 gives a budget of 'I do not know, not much', one owner hour a week and zero team hours; q55 answered 'Uncertain'.

assessment.owner_objective: More profit and cash flow — lift gross margin from 34% to 39% and get the idle VF-4 earning, without adding overhead the shop cannot carry.
assessment.owner_belief: I cannot find machinists. That is it, that is the whole story. There is a VF-4 in the corner that has not cut a chip in fourteen months because there is nobody to stand in front of it. Every problem this shop has traces back to that.
assessment.primary_constraint: Every price in the shop comes out of one person's head against a rate sheet written in March 2021, and the quote that carries it takes eleven days — so the shop wins a quarter of what it quotes, and wins it at rates that predate a 19% rise in the labor those jobs consume.
assessment.constraint_symptoms: Block 2: eleven-day average quote turnaround against two aerospace buyers who award at three, and 26% close on $6.4M of quoted dollars. Block 3: the rate sheet was last modified March 2021 while the P&L shows direct labor up 19% since. Block 4: 9.7 h/wk of quote assembly split between a $88 owner hour and a $36 office hour, and one built in front of us took 2 hours 25 minutes. Block 5: q51 puts pricing history 'in my head and in a drawer'. Four blocks; the rule requires two.
assessment.constraint_cost: ~$47K of contribution a year absorbed by a shop rate unchanged since March 2021 against a 19% rise in direct labor (P&L and rate sheet, Doc) · ~$56K of contribution on quoted work lost to turnaround (RFQ summary, Doc: 26% close at an 11-day average in a 3-day market) · 504 owner-and-estimator hours a year assembling quote packages by hand.
assessment.constraint_fix: Run the job-costing report JobBOSS has been collecting data for since 2016, rebuild the machine-hour rates from what the work actually costs now, and turn quoting into a repeatable package Dana can produce from a part-family template with Walt reviewing rather than originating. Three days is achievable without hiring anybody.
assessment.momentum_initiative: Raise the rate on prototype and short-run work. It is the highest-margin line at 41%, the least price-sensitive, entirely in Walt's control, it needs no system, and it shows in the P&L inside 60 days.

opportunities.title: Rebuild the shop rate from what the work costs now
opportunities.finding: The rate sheet was last modified March 2021 (Doc). The same 24-month P&L shows direct labor up 19% since it was written, and the job-costing report that would have caught this has never been run despite JobBOSS collecting the hours the whole time. Production CNC is $2.32M of the $4.02M at a stated 33% margin — the largest line and the lowest margin in the shop.
opportunities.blueprint: Run the job-costing report against twelve months of collected hours, rebuild machine-hour rates per work centre, and apply the new rates on the next blanket PO renewal in renewal order. Delvane at 22% goes last, after two smaller blankets have proved the conversation. The parts the model shows are being run below cost get quoted at cost or walked away from deliberately, which is where the modelled volume loss comes from.
opportunities.replaces: A five-year-old rate sheet, and the annual habit of renewing a blanket at last year's number.

opportunities.title: Get the quote out in three days instead of eleven
opportunities.finding: $6.4M of RFQ dollars a year close at 26% (Doc). The recorded loss reason is price and lateness, and two aerospace buyers award to whoever answers in three days. Every quote is originated by one 63-year-old estimator working through a physical stack; one built in front of us took 2 hours 25 minutes and was priced from the 2021 sheet.
opportunities.blueprint: Build part-family quote templates from the rebuilt rates so Dana originates the quote and Walt reviews it rather than starting it. Set a three-day service level on the RFQ log with a visible ageing list. Incremental cost is carried at 5% for the overtime the added work absorbs before the VF-4 is staffed.
opportunities.replaces: A paper stack on one desk, and an eleven-day answer in a three-day market.

opportunities.title: Take the quote package off two people's hands
opportunities.finding: 9.7 h/wk — the largest line in the repetitive-work inventory and the only one that touches margin — is quote package assembly split between the owner at a $88 loaded rate and the office at $36. It is flagged for errors, it is the slowest step in the sales cycle, and JobBOSS already holds the cycle times and material costs that most of it re-derives by hand.
opportunities.blueprint: Part-family templates pulling cycle times and material from JobBOSS history, a standing setup and burden table, and an approval step rather than an origination step for the owner. Loaded rate is blended at $46 across the $88 owner hour and the $36 office hour in the proportions the inventory records. Recovered owner hours go to the floor and to customer conversations, which is where q5 says he wants them.
opportunities.replaces: 504 hours a year of print reading, cycle-time arithmetic and spreadsheet building done twice for every part family the shop has quoted before.

expected_blockers: Leverage pillar is insufficient data: four N/As (L6, L7, L9, L10) against the Rubrics v2 §1 threshold of four or more. The pillar must be excluded from the composite and the remaining weights renormalised — Profit 0.40 and Systems 0.35 over 0.75.

The four Leverage N/As are invalid under Rubrics v2 §5: every reason recorded is an absence of the practice ('we don't do AI', 'nothing to govern', 'the team isn't going to use these tools', 'we're not doing a technology project'), not a reason the indicator cannot apply to a 26-person machine shop. The don't-know rule applies instead — score the lowest anchor the evidence supports (q46 'None' supports L6 = 0; q47 empty supports L7 = 0; q58 'No training, and there is resistance' supports L9 = 0; q49 and q55 support L10 = 0 or 1) and flag each as Reported.
Release is blocked until L6, L7, L9 and L10 are rescored or each N/A carries a model-based reason a reviewer will sign.
expected_warnings: an automation-hours opportunity is included in the report while the Leverage pillar it belongs to has been excluded as insufficient data — the reviewer should reconcile the two before delivery
